utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with Ms. Joanne Richardson and Mrs. Patricia Sellers, as co-counsels, and also our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us here today our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. So let me start from here, even though the documents that I will be referring to were filed confidential. You will recall that we last sat on Wednesday -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be Tuesday that we sat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we sat on Tuesday. Yes, we sat on Tuesday. And on my way to the airport, I was informed, to my surprise I must say, at the time, because we had been sitting until the previous day, that Mr. Jones had, on behalf of the Defence, approached a member of my staff, of our staff rather, and informed him that he was objecting to the Prosecution interviewing one of the Defence witnesses, who is due to give evidence shortly, on the assumption that what the Prosecution intended to do was irregular. To cut it short, between the exchanges that I had with my member of the staff, more than one member of the staff, and that included the Senior Legal Officer, in consultation also with the other two Judges, we managed to find out that indeed the Prosecution was intending to interview a Defence witness before, as the Defence put it, the Defence had a chance to proof this witness. And we obtained the assurance on the part of the Prosecution that we -- they would not proceed with this interview, as planned, but wait until the matter is discussed, debated, argued, and decided upon by this Trial Chamber. And in fact, an order was signed by one of the Judges on my behalf precisely specifying this. This morning when I returned to my -- to work, I found a voice message from Mr. Jones, which I would imagine goes back to either Tuesday or Wednesday, in which, to my surprise - and also, I must say, to the surprise of my two colleagues who have heard the voice message - it transpired that what triggered this up in the first place was the understanding on the part of Mr. Jones that there had been an ex parte motion by the Prosecution of which, contrary to normal practice that we have adopted, we did not give notice to the Defence, and that following this ex parte motion, we ordered or we authorised, we issued an order, authorising the Prosecution to interview this individual, as per the ex parte motion. I need to declare here, and I think now the parties do agree that there must have been some misunderstanding between them. I must declare, however, that there was no ex parte motion, such ex parte motion, that there was no discussion at all between the Trial Chamber or any component of the Trial Chamber with the Prosecution with regard to this witness, except what I said earlier. And that we never gave any such order, as I was given to understand when I heard the telephone voice mail. So that is what I wanted to make clear, that there was no ex parte motion. If there had been, we would have followed the previous practice of informing the other party of the existence of such motion. And consequently, and naturally, there couldn't have been any decision on our part. Having said that, I don't know if you are prepared to discuss this matter today; in other words, the substance of the motion and response to that motion that followed, namely a motion by the Defence to prohibit basically the Prosecution from interviewing this individual. Or whether, considering that there is a witness who is an ambassador and who needs to possibly finish his testimony today, you are prepared to postpone it until tomorrow. That is something that I want to hear. But however, I must point out, Mr. Jones, that in exchange for the Prosecution's agreement to postpone this interview until we have discussed it and decided upon it, we promised that we would give the Prosecution and you, of course, the opportunity to debate it and ask to consider it and then decide it. So -- but of course, we are very anxious to know exactly what you intend doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it was just on that procedural matter, really, that, firstly, as Your Honour has rightly observed, we do have an ambassador who's testifying today and who we envisaged would finish today. And he's got travel plans tomorrow. He's of course willing, if necessary, to change those plans. But we did hope to start and finish his testimony today. I can be two to two and a half hours. So that would fit in. That's why I would prefer to discuss it tomorrow. But also for a second reason, which is that according to Your Honour's order, the Prosecution was ordered to file a response on Friday. We were informed by the Prosecution at 4.30 p.m. on Friday that they filed a response. We haven't seen anything in writing, and therefore that's another reason why we're not in a position to reply, particularly if they bring forward any legal arguments or legal authority. We of course need to look into it and need to research any authority. So we would definitely concur with the suggestion that this be postponed until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't seen the response either -- I mean, I haven't seen the response either. I'm not saying that it wasn't filed of course. I'm saying that we haven't seen it. At least, I speak for myself, because I -- what we have been in camera discussing amongst ourselves already, some -- at least what is involved in this issue by a matter of principle and practice, but we were not made aware of your response. In fact, I thought that you were coming over here and say, this is our response or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we filed, indeed, Friday late. And for myself, I also were not able -- was not able to even get a copy from that filing itself. So I can imagine, indeed, that Defence has a right to prepare itself. And secondly, we support, of course, expeditious processing of such a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously, obviously. So I think we will postpone the discussion on this subject. May I also have your agreement, both parties, to postpone discussion on the other motions that we have received, such as Rule 90, such as documents from Republika Srpska, special division, and so on. We'll postpone them until another day? Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If it means that you mean oral discussion or do you -- does that include a written response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You obviously have a right to file, especially with regard to the -- to both of them, actually, both the Ruth 90, et cetera. But Mr. Wubben, and Madam Vidovic, and Mr. Jones, we cannot allow ourselves anymore the luxury of granting ourselves the full time period that we have at our disposal under the Rules. I think if we really need and have to move forward at -- at a reasonable pace, we should cut down on the time limits considerably and try to deal with these motions as expeditiously as possible, because otherwise if I wait for 15 days here, you know, I mean, in the meantime we will be hearing two, three more witnesses and we will be going into recess. So please try to understand that when I say "cut down on the time limits," it's not to the deprive you of the time that you require to answer -- to respond to motions but to insist or impress on you the importance of trying our level best to cut down on the time we need to respond to these motions. This is an appeal that I make, of course. And then if there are problems, like you did last week when you asked for a small extension of time to be able to file one of the responses, I mean we are not unreasonable. We do grant, we do grant. But please try, both of you, to do your level best to come forward with your responses at the shortest time possible. All right. This sitting, today's sitting, I agree entirely with you that we should try to finish with this witness. Have you got an idea how much time you require for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll certainly try and keep within the Trial Chamber's understanding that this is an important witness, first of all, and try and have him finish today. I understand from what the Defence has represented they'll take two and a half hours. By that understanding it appears that I should have at least an hour and time for whatever questions on rejoinder. My cross-examination at this point should fit within that frame, Your Honour, but I do have to just have one caveat, and that is of course seeing the Defence present their evidence might alter the cross-examination; that's just very natural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Can I suggest to you, Mr. Jones, because I see that you will be dealing with this witness, that you try and finish in two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll go as fast I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I, in that regard I take it that on uncontentious matters and broadly construed uncontentious matters of the Security Council, et cetera, that I can lead a fair bit of the evidence. That way we will obviously go a lot quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Unless -- we will adopt the usual practice. Unless I have serious objections from the other party, we will not intervene as you put direct questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I might just say that this witness has testified in the Milosevic case. He's -- he gave a very lengthy statement to the Prosecution. He's an ambassador of many years experience, and so the risk of suggestion, I submit, is minimal to non-existent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is he still an ambassador? I'm asking that so I know how to address him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think he still has the benefit of that title but is not serving as an ambassador currently, so....

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just say, Your Honour, we'll enter into the merits tomorrow of this whole matter, but just I apologise that you had to come back to a voice mail message from me. As you understand, on that Tuesday evening we were trying to reach various people, and it was expedient for me to leave a message, after subsequently I thought of retracting the message or leaving another message, but I thought it best just to leave it as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two very short submissions to do. It's about producing documents already promised and information regarding completing a Prosecution exhibit. Can that be done in the meanwhile while the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you do it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I can do it quickly, Your Honours. It's about the letter by Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio on the 21st of October, 2005. I want to tender it, because it has to deal with the Simic article and should be confirmed officially through tendering. And I would like to tender it and ask for a P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the next Prosecution exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P610, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that document will become P610. And what's the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The other issue is notification that we had problems with two videos, part of videos, P3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that can wait until tomorrow, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's just an announcement that we solved it, but we will tender new copies to the Judges by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, we don't know what this is, P610, and the Simic article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know either, Mr. Jones. We will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So we will reserve our observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is the witness? In fact, can we see this document, P610, what it is all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ambassador, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. I know it's not the first time you've been asked to give evidence, but of course I -- as Presiding Judge I would like to welcome you again. My name is Carmel Agius. I come from Malta and I am the Presiding Judge in this trial against Naser Oric. I am flanked to my right by Judge Hans Hendrik Brydensholt from the Kingdom of Denmark, and on my left by Judge Professor Albin Eser from Germany. So welcome. You know what the procedure is. You are going to start giving evidence very shortly, and before you do that our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the solemn declaration that is contained in the text that is being handed to you now. Please read that text aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ambassador. Please make yourself comfortable. Ambassador, how would you like us to address you? Usually I address ambassadors here in The Hague and elsewhere as Your Excellency. How would you like me to address you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please refrain from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are a Defence witness, and it will be Mr. Jones who will go first. We are trying to do our best to finish with your testimony today so that you can fly back tomorrow, as scheduled. I have the cooperation of both parties in trying to do that. So Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Please give your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Diego Enrique Arria.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now, confirm for me, if you will, the following details. Firstly, you were born on the 8th of October, 1938, and are of Venezuelan nationality?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And your career has been as a politician, diplomat, and ambassador?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're currently a consultant and visiting scholar of Columbia University in New York?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll pause occasionally for the interpretation. And you're also special advisor to the Secretary-General of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, is it right that you were the permanent representative of Venezuela at the United Nations from 1991 to 1993, serving in the Security Council after Venezuela's election as a non-permanent member in 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I just need a few more details to confirm. In March 1992 you served as the president of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In April 1993 you were the coordinator of the caucus of the non-aligned countries represented in the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact, I think it's true to say, isn't it, that you were a co-sponsor with France and the United States in the resolution establishing this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. I was very proud of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now speaking about this Tribunal, did you testify here in the Milosevic case on the 10th of February, 2004?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you testified as a witness for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In preparing for that testimony, were you interviewed by the Prosecution in April 2003 and again in September 2003?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as a result of that, was a witness statement drawn up?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to pass up an exhibit which is the statement from 2003. I trust we can safely ignore that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. We don't have to worry about this because this is the usual siren tests on Monday at noon. So that's why I looked at my watch, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's no need to run from the building, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Thank you. I wasn't planning to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, what you have in front of you is a witness statement with a witness information cover sheet, and it's a statement comprising 68 pages and 495 paragraphs. Do you recognise that as the statement that was drawn up, following your interview?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you review this statement in detail over the last two days?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And are the contents of that statement true to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we're going to go to some passages in that statement, but for the sake of context the statement concerns the policy and inaction, action or inaction, of the UN and UN member states to the Bosnian conflict in 1992/1993, when you were sitting in the Security Council as the permanent representative of Venezuela. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As well as comments on the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995 and the responsibility of the UN and UN member states for that tragedy. It also contains those comments?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, following Venezuela's election to the Security Council, were you involved in briefings on the situation in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And who were some of the people you had contacts with or who you spoke to and gained information?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You mean within the United Nations or outside the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was thinking initially within the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conflict in 1992, the secretariat was basically the main source of information on the developments on the ground. That changed very rapidly when the secretariat was not so forthcoming and so opportune in reporting to the Security Council. And I would say that the international media replaced the secretariat largely by providing objective, factual, and opportune reporting and information to the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And even prior to the beginning of the conflict or as it started, did you have contact with Darko Silovic, the ambassador to the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. Because Ambassador Silovic was the head of the non-aligned movement in the United Nations, was at the time the former Yugoslavia ambassador to the UN, a very respected diplomat. And as I stated in Mr. Milosevic's trial, the non-aligned -- we were against the partition of the former Yugoslavia. We actually cooperated with the then-foreign minister Loncar of Croatia, a Croat Yugoslav, to promote within the international community, mainly the European community, not to fragment former Yugoslavia. Mr. Milosevic asked me here when did I -- or when did we change our mind about that, and I responded that it took very few weeks for the international community to find out that Mr. Milosevic was not joso bros [phoen] Tito, and that he was already placing former Yugoslavia under great peril and danger as had proven to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in the interests of time, we're going to attempt to summarise the main points of your statement, which we have -- which you have in front of you. And first I want to ask you about the arms embargo on the former Yugoslavia and its effect. And I refer to paragraphs 57 to 73 of your statement dealing with Resolution 740 of 7 February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Paragraphs 57 to 73. It's page 10 and onwards. And firstly, Security Council Resolution 740 of 7 February, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I would just like to offer this broad objection. Also I understand the questions of timing, but certainly it appears as if Ambassador Arria either has current memory of the situation, what he's testified to, and at this point the statement, I don't understand whether it's refreshing recollection that he no longer has or he's going to testify about something and then the statement confirms that that was also his contemporaneous understanding or he's testified about it before. But just to show, in essence, I believe the statement is now being used to lead the evidence in this sense and not corroborate evidence that the ambassador has. I say that knowingly within type of time constraints that we are in, but I would like to state that for the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. What's your position on this, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, two points. Firstly I haven't even started using it yet, so I don't see how Ms. Sellers is making a timely objection. She should wait and see. But secondly the Prosecution can't have their cake and eat it, too, as far as this is concerned. We are all, apparently, trying to make an effort to finish with this witness today. Now, if I don't use an exhibit which this witness has said he has perused over the last two days, it's true to the best of his knowledge and belief, then we can be here for a week. I can ask him non-leading questions about Security Council Resolutions, and I really don't see the purpose of that. So as I say, the Prosecution is trying to have their cake and eat it, too, in laying down an objection, which now I suppose they'll seek to rely on in due course, but at the same time insist that I go speedily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Our position is as follows. I think the way it should go logically and in a legal context should be the following: That if you intend to tender this in evidence as an exhibit, I think -- you are fully entitled to do that, that's number one, because it's a statement released to the Prosecution. That's number one. The understanding is that this of course is not in substitution of his evidence. He's testifying viva voce here. So you should put the -- to the witness, first and foremost, whether he stands by what is contained here, in other words, whether he confirms on oath, or pursuant to his solemn declaration, the contents -- the correctness of the contents of this statement. If he does, then I -- of course you are entitled to put to him any questions which go beyond or arise out of the contents of this statement. But possibly, please try to avoid asking him to confirm bits and pieces of this statement, because if he confirms the entirety of it he doesn't need to confirm every event as we go along, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is basically our approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask him to elaborate on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, elaborate and answer any other questions that you would have for him. But -- I mean, we can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, Your Honour. I might observe, by the way, that this statement was in front of Ambassador Arria when he gave evidence in Milosevic as an aide-memoire. I find it a bit curious, to say the least, that the Prosecution is seeking to take a different approach in this case, but there you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ambassador, could you -- firstly, yes. I asked you earlier in fact if you confirmed that this statement was true to the best of your knowledge and belief. Would you actually affirm on oath the truth of what's contained in this statement in all of the paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I absolutely do. I guess you are referring to the whole document or to the specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The whole document.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely, I certainly do. I have re-read it several times. I prepared very well my intervention last time in the Milosevic case. I fully believe in that then and I fully believe it in now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And indeed, in terms of using this document, I think it can't hardly be expected for a witness to remember every single date, et cetera, and that's why it's very natural that this should be used as an aid for the witness in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As we go along, yes, of course, by all means, Mr. Jones. But what we meant is don't read out paragraph 53, for example, to the witness, to the Ambassador, and then tell him: Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go a step further straight away. And if he needs to refer to the -- to his statement, of course once he has confirmed it has, he every right to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now at the time of passing the resolution, which imposed an arms embargo, did you think it would stop the war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, we very naively thought that that was the case. When I say "we naively thought that that was the case," I refer to the non-permanent members of the Security Council at the time that didn't have the same information as the permanent members in the secretariat had on the real situation on the ground in reference to how fully armed one side of Yugoslavia was against another party who was completely unarmed. I thought at the time that we were doing the right thing. Later on, a few months later, we found out the real truth. And I always maintain, Your Honours, that with that decision the main members of the Security Council, with the support of the secretariat, decided the outcome of the conflict, in which one party was supposed to roll over the other one very rapidly because it was armed. And the other party was supposed to roll over and play dead. But the Bosniaks were not very good active of that play, for that script, and did not roll over and play dead. They resisted, which became a process of massacre and murders and acts of atrocities against them from then on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. So you say "one party was supposed to roll over and play dead," and you referred to the Bosniaks in that regard. And just for the record, the party which was expected to win rapidly, which side was that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was undoubtedly what was left of former Yugoslavia, which was the Serbian part under Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was admitted as a member of the United Nations in March 1992. Now, is it right firstly that under the United Nations' charter it is the right of self-defence?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies. It's because I -- now I'm anxious about referring to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's very disruptive, Your Honour. I'm going to continue as I planned initially, Your Honour, and hopefully there will be no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I refer to paragraph 60 of your statement you say there pretty much what you've just told us now. I'm going to read two sentences from there. "Little did we know then that with that resolution we were involuntarily deciding the outcome of the conflict, that we were sealing the fate of the Bosnian republic, that we were taking away from this member country the right of self-defence enshrined in the UN charter. What seemed a moral act was in fact the equivalent of what, with hindsight, looks like a premeditated death sentence for the Bosnian Muslim 'side' of the Bosnian and Herzegovina republic." Now, firstly I'll ask you to explain a little why you say it was a premeditated death sentence.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I said at the time when this was discussed in the Security Council that I could not imagine that the permanent members of the Security Council, which were the most powerful members of the international community in the secretariat, didn't know that the Serb party had left all this armament on the republic of what became the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the Bosniak part were completely disarmed and didn't even have an army, didn't have a regular army, which I think the closer thing to a regular army that they had was at the end of the conflict, probably after 1994, but not before when they were more what the French call a levee en masse, people that were resistant, like the Maquis in France, disorganised and weak and disarmed. That's what I meant at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And why do you say the "Bosnian Muslim side," with "side" in inverted commas?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In paragraph 60, if you see the last sentence, you say: "The Bosnian Muslim" -- and the "side" in inverted commas. Why do you put "side" in inverted commas, if you can explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was always very puzzled at the United Nations' behaviour and the international community. Before 1991 I never heard or read that the -- that when they addressed the Bosniaks they referred to them as Muslims. This started after Serbia invaded Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then someone in the international community seemed to have discovered there were Muslims there. It used to be Bosniaks for hundreds of years. Suddenly the creation of an ethnic element was included into the whole equation which make it sound even much more confusing and terrible than it was, and the way some people have at the time, and later on, presented like in the former Yugoslavia was integrated where three tribes of savages, Croats, Serbs, and Bosniaks, which was not the case. The fact that some of the people and the leaders had behaved bestially didn't mean that the people were like that. But suddenly this ethnic issue became a fundamental element into the whole discussion, and I believe that distorted the perception of a simple fact that a fanatic in Serbia who had invaded a territory of a member of the United Nations, and then the international community would not raise a finger to defend that, not to protect them, and would not allow them to arm themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, if you turn to the next page of your statement at paragraph 66, there's a reference to "a fear that Bosnia-Herzegovina would become the tar baby of Europe." Now, can you explain that expression for us. What was that about?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I had -- I was not familiar with that expression until one permanent member of the Security Council said it to me. Later on I found out as a part of the Africa folklore captured by a historic story-teller in America which explains that when you find yourself in a inexplicable situation that you cannot get away from, that you're caught in a situation. And the reference that I made there that this ambassador made to me, it was a fear that the European, some of the main European countries, were afraid to bring this conflict to Europe. But it was in Europe. But nevertheless, they didn't want to get involved in the conflict. And they thought that the Serbs would rapidly go over the rest of the country and peace will be secured in that part of Europe. Part of this was - and I have said it before - that the Europeans never considered the Bosniaks as Europeans but suddenly considered them as Muslims, which they had not done before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to explore something you say at paragraph 92 of your statement, which is at page 14, and for the sake of context I do need to read. Paragraph 92: "On 8 June 1992 I attended the UNSC when UNSC Resolution 758 was approved. The resolution reflected a cynical interpretation of reality by requesting the victims not to impede the delivery of humanitarian aid to themselves by the reference to, 'all the parties and others concerned'- victims and aggressors were considered alike." Now, can you explain what you mean by that phrase, "victims and aggressors were considered alike."

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, one of the most reprehensible behaviours of the international community that I found in the Security Council was always to try to reach the moral equivalence of the parties. Because if you treat both as criminals, as responsible, then you don't make any difference between them. Then there is no moral obligation on your part to participate. While at the same time, had you acknowledged that there was one aggressor against a member country of the United Nations, by the charter the Security Council would have been obligated and forced to act. But because they don't want to act, it was much better to ignore it and to cover up the whole problem as the parties, which is a really not only a euphemism, but a perverse way to describe the reality that was happening. That's what I meant with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And who in this scenario were the victims and who were the aggressors?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The aggressor was, obviously, the groups within Serbia -- within Bosnia-Herzegovina, I'm sorry, that were financed, supported, aided, armed by the former Republic of Yugoslavia. And the victims were the people on one part, some parts of Croatia, and then Bosnia-Herzegovina where the concentrated attacks and acts of vandalisms took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that regard, we have the next exhibit which is going to be distributed. It's a United Nations Security Council document. It's for general distribution. S/24377, 4 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do this one by one. First I think we need to give an exhibit number to the Ambassador's statement that you are referring him to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the next Defence exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D951, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be D951. And the new document that you are seeking to tender or to introduce in the records will be D952.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, this is a letter dated 4 August, 1992, from the permanent representative of Venezuela to the United Nations addressed to the President of the Security Council. "There have been reports in the international communication media about concentration camps and the torture of citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by citizens of the federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Clearly, in view of their nature, these atrocities committed by citizens of one country against another, which is also a member of our organisation, cannot be regarded as internal acts that violate human rights but rather as inhuman acts of aggression by one country against another which continue to constitute a serious threat to international peace and security."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's signed by yourself. Do you recall this, Ambassador, this letter?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I do. I recall it with sadness, because even though when I wrote that letter to the President of the Security Council it was because the international media had projected in colours to the world to see that there were concentration camps and torture, the United Nations at the time never produced a report, not even mentioning that fact. I certainly -- and the UN Security Council did not act in that occasion pertaining to my letter and to my request that the Security Council addressed such a grave violation of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And so you considered at this point that this was actually an ingression by one country against another?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely. That was precisely the whole -- the essence of that, even though at the time the Red Cross and many other NGOs had already reported it. It was even actually officially reported by then-President Izetbegovic of Bosnia to the President Francois Mitterrand at the time. And even though all those negotiations were made and presented, no one did anything about it. It took years to actually discover what was really happening in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we have a new exhibit now which is -- yes, it's called "professionalism in war reporting, a correspondent's view." It's by Tom Gjelten from the Carnagie Commission on Preventing Deadly Conflict dated September 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about a few opinions expressed here. Now firstly I'm going to direct your attention to the first page, the third paragraph. And this is, as we can see from the context, it concerns the Bosnian conflict. And it says, paragraph 3: "Instinctively many of the UN officers," and this is in Bosnia, "felt more at ease among Serb army commanders who were career military men and treated them respectfully than among Muslim commanders, few of whom had military training." I want to ask you: Is that something you came across in relation to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had the privilege to lead the Security Council mission to Srebrenica, which was the first time in the history of the United Nations that the UN Security Council mission would go to the ground during a conflict. And when I got to Srebrenica, I knew why the UN Security Council would never send mission to the ground, because you discover the truth was taking place that is being covered up behind documents and papers and statements. One thing we discovered -- I was shocked to find out when after many struggles to try to go into Srebrenica, being obstructed, sabotaged by the second in command of the UNPROFOR forces, Brigadier Hayes, which prevented the arrival of about 40 international journalists who were accompanying our mission were left stranded in Zvornik, was that when we entered Srebrenica -- I entered first with Hayes and some of the Canadian officers. There was a group, to my surprise, within Srebrenica of Serb officials. At that time, we in the Security Council thought that Srebrenica was under siege, but we didn't know that it had been capitulated with the cooperation of the United Nations Protection Forces. I was surprised to see these Serb officials next to Brigadier Hayes. And then there was a group of civilians, and Brigadier Hayes proceeded to introduce them to me. And he said, if my memory doesn't failed me, it's Colonel, Radic or Rodic, basically lieutenant colonel such-and-such and such-and-such of the Republic of Srpksa. And I say, What is that? Well, you know, this is the Serb Republic of Srpksa. I said, We don't have at the United Nations any republic that we recognise with that name. He proceeded to identify the five or six officers from the Serb side, and then he looked at the civilians who are on the other side, all kinds of -- one had a green shirt, another brown, and he said, Well, and these are also my friends. "These also my friends" were the Bosnian representatives of the insurgency -- or the resistance in Bosnia. It was obvious that he considered the Serb, Srpksa Serbs, officials, like the real authorities, the formal authorities, and he considered the Bosniaks, whose country he was in, as sort of egregious or insurgents but not as authoritative. So I was shocked to see how they acknowledge the aggressors of the official authorities and the victims as the opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we have the date of this mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, we're going to come to that subsequently, but the Ambassador can tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When was your mission?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: That was in March 1993. It is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can refer to --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I think it is 24th, but I will have to check. It is in the latter part of March. It was the -- Your Honours, probably I may add that this mission was prompted when the five members of the Security Council, what they call at the time the non-aligned group, was watching television how the village of Srebrenica was under siege. And then at the time the Pakistani ambassador, Marker, presided the Council, and we pressed the council to send a mission because the secretariat wasn't informing or reporting to us. CNN, BBC, Reuters, were the source of information. I said at the time that the least informed body at the time officially and institutionally was the Security Council because information was used as a weapon to really obstruct to view the realities on the ground. Actually, when we were discussing the resolution to declare Srebrenica a safe area, actually we wanted it to be a protected area, what we were discussing at 2.00 in the morning in New York, thinking that we are going to save Srebrenica, on the ground in Sarajevo the UNPROFOR forces were hoping to capitulate and to force a rendition of that village, which we only discovered a few days later when we got to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. We're going to come to your mission shortly and we'll have the report so we can check the exact date. But you mentioned Brigadier Hayes a moment ago, and if you turn to page 4, second paragraph of this it says: "To the news media in Bosnia with no professional obligation to satisfy one side or another, it sometimes appeared that UNPROFOR commanders were misrepresenting reality in their eagerness to maintain good relations with the Serb side. A good example was the effort by UNPROFOR commanders to promote the notion that Sarajevo was not actually besieged because the Serb forces that encircled the city occasionally let UN convoys proceed through their lines. 'There is no humanitarian seige,' declared Brigadier Vere Hayes, Chief of Staff to the UNPROFOR commander in Bosnia, speaking in Sarajevo in August 1993." I just wanted to ask you if that's the same Brigadier Hayes you're referring to and if you recall this incident.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I certainly do. Your Honours, in a country like Bosnia, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, its deputy prime minister, if I pronounce it correctly, Mr. Turajlic, was assassinated while travelling in the United Nations Protection Forces' armoured car under the alleged protection of a French officer, is shot in daylight, and no one knows anything about it, and the officer gets promoted in France, you -- the message is: You can clearly get away with murder. While Sarajevo -- Sarajevo had been few years before the host of the Olympic Winter Games, and it was -- told the world that it was an extraordinary event. There were no savages there. It was a most ecumenical city, probably one of the most ecumenical cities in the world, and the whole world was happy to be there. When it became -- when Brigadier Hayes was not under siege, some of you must know that the only communication that Sarajevo had at the end was under a tunnel built under the airport strip. And the UNPROFOR forces tried many times to sink this tunnel because they were afraid that the tunnel would endanger the United Nations forces at the airport. I remember Vice-President Ganic of Bosnia telling me that every time he was asked by Hayes and Rose, General Hayes and Rose, what where the noises under the ground, he would say, Well, we are building 50 tunnels at the same time in all kinds of directions in order to divert. That was the only way, the only link of communication. If it has not been under siege, I really cannot understand the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And was in fact -- are you aware whether Brigadier Hayes was criticised even by Madeleine Albright for those remarks?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier Hayes behaved more like a subordinate to the Serb side in Bosnia than as a real officer. We were surprised, the mission, to see how respectful he was with the Serb side and how disrespectful he was with the country that was hosting him. He said in the New York Times at the moment that the United Nations Security Council Resolutions were really hated. Actually he said that to me the first day when we got there in Sarajevo. He said, Every time I hear you speaking on BBC on the issue of Sarajevo, I feel like calling you and telling you that these solutions are really hated. And I said, Well, General, I think you had done that, if that would not have been possible, because you would have been first to report to your boss, and your boss to the other one, and then to the Secretary-General, and then to me. But I don't know whether it's pertinent or not, but with the same context I read in one of your witnesses in this trial that even Morillon, General Morillon, referred to the people in Srebrenica as "those nest of terrorists." And that coming from the mouth of a distinguished French officer is really very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's an exhibit we're going to come to shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number for this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will become Defence Exhibit D953.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And the next exhibit which we have is a draft of the International Human Rights Law Institute chronology of the battle and siege of Sarajevo 03503839 to 03504242. And it's volume 1, part B, January 1993 to September 1993. This is a selection of pages. We're not exhibiting the whole volume, which would be voluminous.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But if you turn to page 3 of this bundle, and it's 03504193.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The third page in the second paragraph. And we see in there: "British Brigadier General Hayes, Chief of Staff of UN forces in Bosnia, told reporters in the Bosnian capital that the Bosnian army bore the main blame of blocking relief supplies to Sarajevo. He said the current assault on Mount Igman was strangling only the Bosnian military supply line into Sarajevo." So here it appears, the third page, second paragraph, it says 03504193 at the top page. On the front "draft of the international human rights law."

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I don't see which paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can pass up my copy. "British Brigadier General Hayes, Chief of Staff of the UN forces." Let me provide my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to go on the record, and that's with a document we have before us. I can appreciate Defence counsel's offer. I would have to ask that we would see whatever he would pass up to a witness while a witness was testifying about an exhibit, although I believe it will probably show that paragraph marked. And the other I was wondering whether Your Honour would like to have any of these documents placed on the ELMO so that the public can see what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Certainly this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have the paragraph now, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, have you seen the paragraph which I was referring to?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. The one referring to Brigadier Hayes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, yes, I remember this well. It was referring that this -- the Bosnians inside its own country were making life very difficult for them to take -- for the Serbs to take the city of Sarajevo. And that was really the most cynical accusation, to call the victims aggressors.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we turn to the second-to-last page of this document --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Second one?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Second-to-last page and it says 03504227. It says: "According to US Ambassador Madeleine Albright, UN Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali accepted a US complaint that two UN peacekeeping officers, Brigadier General Hayes, Chief of Staff of the command of UNPROFOR, and Lieutenant Colonel Barry Frewer, the Sarajevo spokesman of UNPROFOR, made inappropriate remarks. Hayes and Frewer had told reporters that Sarajevo was no longer under siege but was encircled by the Serbs." I end the quote there. Do so you agree, that that's a very perverse picture which was drawn by Brigadier Hayes and that he was reprimanded by Madeleine Albright for those remarks?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case that Brigadier Hayes also criticise President Clinton and said, What does he think he is? For referring to this situation. And this is not only perverse but a cruel way to describe a city that was being under siege and under attack. Well, in that context even Boutros-Ghali said that he knew of about ten more other cities in the world that were having a worse situation than Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this was typical of a certain attitude of the -- on the part of the United Nations towards the conflict, to downplay the seriousness?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, it also much saw the case that, Your Honours, I ask you to imagine a United Nations Security Council mission that started at 4.00 in the afternoon and the meeting ended at 3.00 in the morning, seriously discussing how to protect the city of Srebrenica, while at the same time -- and actually, they ended before, like I said, the United Nations forces on the ground had capitulated Srebrenica. I remember that later on the president -- the vice-president of Bosnia, Anic, told me that in the wee hours of the morning at the airport to Sarajevo, Brigadier Hayes said to General Halilovic, General, is it time for you to kneel down? Let's pray? And brought down his Bible to the Bosnian commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The Bosnian commander being a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask for an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Jones, will become D954. And I recognise Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to point out in this document, and counsel might be able to assist us. It appears to be a document where the numbering, the pagination, at least within the ERNs, is irregular. I just want to make it clear that the Defence is submitting these distinct pages with the ERN number and not the document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I thought I said that before. This is a selection of pages, and of course the Prosecution has access to the full document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this, I take it, is a document that was given to you or made available to you by the Prosecution itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That I can't answer offhand, but I imagine it might be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But for the record, let me enter now the ERN numbers that I see on this document. First one, which is title page, is 03503839. The second page is 03504192. The third, 03504193. The next page is 03504215. Next is 03504216. And then we have 03504220. Next is 221, the next is 225, the next is 227, and the last one is 242. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to a matter covered in your statement, and just -- well, we won't refer to it. But it concerns the fact that the UNHCR, Madam Ogata of Japan, tried to bring the attention of the UN to the plight of Srebrenica back in December 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, during my -- the position in the Mr. Milosevic case, I was presented with a copy of that letter 11 years later, which we never saw in the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to be clear, there's a letter of December 1992 and I think one of March 1993. Did you see either of them at the time?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No. And the serious implication of that is that Madam Ogata, whom I have personally consulted on the issue of how to draft proper guidelines for a safe area, expressly said in the letter to Mr. Boutros-Ghali: I urge you, if I memory doesn't fail me, I urge you to warn the leaders of the West of the emerging and monumental tragedy that might occur in Srebrenica. That, by itself, should have been a very powerful alarm in the Security Council. This letter came to my attention 11 years later. Why the Secretary-General would not report to the Security Council such a grave warning is something which is very reprehensible. And I have stated, Your Honours, before that that became part, what I believe still is, a major cover-up of the responsibility evaded by the international community, mainly by the main powers represented in the Council, to face the reality of genocide taking place before their own eyes. And to have an official like Madam Ogata, a very distinguished leader in her own country and in the international community, reporting that seriousness was something that could not be swept under the rug, like it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So instead of being swept under the rug, the letter wasn't distributed. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, during the course of being involved in the discussions on Bosnia, did you ever see maps which had been prepared in terms of allocating territory to the different -- to the Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I said in one of my -- it is in the record because I said it in one of my official speeches in the Security Council that a few days after the Security Council welcomed the new member of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina into its midst, we already started a partition process of the same member few weeks afterwards, not even weeks, days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you specifically about Srebrenica. Did you see where Srebrenica was placed on those maps?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. This is the point precisely that I wanted to refer to. In the first Vance-Owen Plan I remember talking to Owen and saying this cartography, exercise in cartography you are doing establishing the partition of a member country, and Srebrenica, which was on the eastern part, is in the eastern part, they considered that it was very close to serve Serbia proper in a way closer to what they called at the time the Greater Serbia, that it was very distant from the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So on the first maps, it was always Srebrenica was always a target of the negotiations as part of the closer area of the enclave closer to Greater Serbia. It was always the case throughout. And today, as we know, Srebrenica is part of that part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you refer to these maps from the Vance-Owen negotiations, what year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: They started at 1992 until the middle of 1993 when Mr. Stoltenberg replaced Mr. Owen and Mr. Vance, and all the negotiations failed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So in 1992 and 1993 there was already a move to put Srebrenica in, as you called it, Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Oh, yes, very much so. It was always a target, not only a military target, it was a diplomatic target.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The next exhibit which is -- it's from the UNHCR dated 18 March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see -- on the one hand, this is a document from the UNHCR, and I'm always now sensitive about any concerns for its circulation. At the same time, this was shown publicly in the Milosevic trial, and you'll see from the nature of the document it's addressed to the Secretary-General. I think it can be safely discussed in open session and placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a position on this, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm rather confused by relating the document to the other trial. Are we trying to say that we would want this to be sealed in this trial for whatever reason the Defence counsel might offer or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- or are we saying this document is just a normal potential Defence exhibit document. I don't understand precisely the nature of Defence counsel's comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All I was saying is I think this can be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the whole issue. To my knowledge, all documents supplied to you by this UN agency is always under the caveat that at any time they may require you not to use them. Now, this document seems to have been given a number. It seems that it has been made use of in another trial. So what I would like to know from you before we proceed any further is whether you have any objection for this document to be made use of in this trial and that it, in addition, be publicly made use of. In other words, if there is a reservation from UNHCR with regard to the use of this document at this trial, we will have to respect it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, normally there's an R in front if it's restricted, whereas there's no R --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I've had to deal with UNHCR in other cases and also in this case, but I don't know what the position is as regards you are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, precisely. Usually that's indicated by an R before the ERN. What I would like to say is that: Could we just reserve this position, and for an abundance of caution at this time period to not place it on the ELMO, have it public, and I will certainly come back to Your Honours by the break just to confirm that we can use it publicly or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. In fact, there's another question that I might ask which can maybe throw some light on this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ambassador, do you see at the top it says the "GlenRock Group"?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that group?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, very much. I am in the board of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in fact did you receive this document?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. Because when I was preparing for the -- Mr. Milosevic's proceedings, I got this letter from the United Nations, and I sent it to -- either to the Prosecutor's office or to one of the investigators. I was -- that's when I noticed that they had the fax, name of the GlenRock Group, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That might help. We won't place it on the ELMO. I will read from it. There is nothing confidential, certainly, in the content. It says: "The situation in the Srebrenica enclave is deteriorating by the hour. The latest reports I've received from my staff on the spot are appalling. Thousands of people entering the town from surrounding areas which have been systematically attacked and taken by Serb forces. People are dying from military action and starvation and lack of medical treatment at a rate of 30 to 40 a day." And then the next page: "Everything would indicate that a massive humanitarian tragedy is unfolding in the Srebrenica enclave. I believe key world leaders should be alerted to these developments." And she requests that the urgent issue be brought to the attention of the Security Council. Now, you've told us -- well, tell us again because I'm not sure if it's this letter. This is dated 18 March 1993. Was this letter brought to your attention in the Security Council at the time?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No, it was not. And that's precisely the point that I did try to make, that for four months the United Nations secretariat, and I am sure the main members, knew what was developing there. But they -- they waited until I think a British journalist from ABC, Birtley, Tony Birtley went into Srebrenica and presented to the world what was happening there. I still remember the faces of some of my colleagues in the Security Council. There was a television set outside the Security Council, watching the people -- what was happening in Srebrenica. And I could not believe that in the body that's supposed to represent international peace and security for humanity was being informed by a commercial station -- at that time was CNN or ABC, and for four months where this was taking place, evolving or deteriorating, no one had done anything. I found that actually criminal behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, also you've told us how you went on a mission to Srebrenica subsequently. Did the conditions there tally or not with the picture painted in this letter?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You know, the situation was even worse. I remember there were five other ambassadors with me, one was a Russian. And I told him, you know, I was in Leningrad recently and I saw the museum and saw the photographs. And I said, I'm sure that watching around you here you must be moved by the tragedy that you are watching. I said, you know, what we have here is a slow-motion genocide taking place under the protection of the United Nations security forces, protection forces. I even said that the -- our offices look more like the capas [phoen] in a concentration camp rather than the protectors of the people. This is a city which I understand had been a skiing village. You only see devastation, burned houses, only women and old men and children in the streets. No water, no electricity, no gas, no doctors. And we had been told that they were under siege and surrounded by Serb tanks all around. It looked like a shooting gallery where the people in the village were down and the Serb tanks surrounded them, that they could shoot them at their own -- at their mercy, at their will. This malice, this stagnancy, it was -- in my whole experience I never seen anything like it. I didn't see one single soldier. I said, you know, they are surrounded, a civilian population. And what was very shocking, Your Honours, I must tell you, I landed in one of the United Nations helicopters in what used to be the soccer field, and I saw about 20 men dressed in white, you know, white robes, like doctors or paramedics, and I asked one of the officers: Are those Medecins Sans Frontieres or the Red Cross? He said: No, they are Serb doctors. I said: What are they doing here? They are doing the triage to see if they will let them out or not of the wounded people, mostly old men. So the United Nations was helping, actually, in the triage to say this one comes in, this one doesn't come out, this one goes in the helicopter, and this one stays here, this one taken, which is exactly what happened two years later when they took 7.000 people out of Srebrenica and murdered them in the same procedure. You get into the bus, you don't get into the bus, you are strike-out, you are dead. It is the coldest, most cruel experience I have seen, and under the United Nations banner. That week, Your Honours, a week before we got there, a bomb -- shells were exploded in the school in Srebrenica. Brigadier Hayes wanted to take us around the town. Fortunately Madam Ogata's representative, a distinguished Spaniard, Mendiluce, later became a member of parliament called me aside and said to me, Ask them to take you to the school, ask them to take you to ex mountain, you will see the tanks. Thanks to him we were able to see the deployment of the tanks. I forced the mission to go to the school. There was still remnants of children had who had been killed a week before. And when I turned around to see what was behind me in the school, this Serb colonel, together with Brigadier Hayes, probably the man who was responsible for shelling these children, was almost hand in hand with the head of the United Nations forces in Srebrenica. And later on, when we went through the town, the two of them were in the United Nations protection forces armoured car, which I found it so reprehensible that we would go into the cities being victimised by the Serbs, and they take a United Nations Security Council mission and parade it through the town with the officer in charge of the destruction, siege and attacks and vandalism of that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can have a break now, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps an exhibit number for this before we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will become Defence Exhibit D955, with the understanding, Ms. Sellers, if you come back to us with problems relating to the publicity of this document, then we will put it under seal of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 30-minute break and then we will have one more session in order to make it possible for us to make the plenary we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We are stopping at 4.00; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, the plenary starts at 4.00, so we will try to stop any time between 3.00 and 3.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm making good progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ambassador, we will have a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your client isn't seated as yet. Yes, Mr. Jones, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, before the break you were telling us, in fact, about your mission to Srebrenica. And now I'm going to just, in the interests of time and clarification, ask a few brief questions which you can probably answer shortly just to set the context. First, who proposed that mission?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was proposed by -- I was the head of the group of the non-aligned at the time in the Security Council. And, yes, I proposed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this -- again, this is described in detail in your statement, so I won't go through that paragraph by paragraph. Did you also -- one moment, please. You proposed it, and were you the head, also, of the mission?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was it the first ever mission undertaken by the Security Council or had there been others before?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was there any opposition to your mission?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. It was quite a struggle within the Security Council for about two hours' discussion. The precedent that this was going to set or not. But finally, we were able to prevail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you carried out the mission, of course. Did you produce a report?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. And I personally drafted the report which was -- then was unanimously agreed by the members of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we're going to pass up copies of the report now. I'm going to take one matter in relation to that report and then come back to it. So this is -- this bears the reference number S/25700 of 30 April 1993. It's a United Nations Security Council document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to state at this time period, and I apologise to Defence counsel for not bringing this up before we began, the testimony in this segment of Ambassador Arria, that the document we referred to earlier, the letter from Ms. Ogata, I have been able to check our sources and it need not be under seal, just in case Defence counsel wanted to use it further during this examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers, and I appreciate your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I also wanted to state on the record that we don't have the letter of December 1992. I state that on the record for various reasons, otherwise I would have used it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, as I said, I'm going to come back to this document later. But firstly, do you recognise this as being the letter of transmittal with your report?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 13 I think we can establish now the actual date that you went to Srebrenica. It says: "Itinerary, annex 1, 25 April 1993, arrival at Srebrenica." I I'm just wondering, could that be correct, that it was actually 25 April 1993? I think you might have said March before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he did say March before. Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is this the correct date, April 1993?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to this document in the course -- and perhaps I could ask for an exhibit number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document will become Defence Exhibit D956.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've already described a number of aspects of your mission, of what occurred. You mentioned Brigadier Hayes obviously a couple of times, and one thing you mentioned that he called Security Council Resolutions on this whole matter woolly-headed. I just want to ask: In your view, was his attitude a factor in why Resolutions were not being implemented in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Security Council Resolutions on --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You know, it would be unfair of me to say that in absolute terms because, after all, Brigadier Hayes had a commanding officer, above him, who was General Morillon. And General Morillon had on top of him the hierarchy General Wahlgren at the time. So it would have to be a collective one. Now, the fact that he was in Sarajevo while Wahlgren was in Zagreb made a significant difference on the ground, but I cannot say that he was alone in that predicament.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it General Wahlgren? Is that who you're referring to in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. His headquarters were in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's where he was based, then, during this time?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. General Morillon was based in Kiseljak, and Brigadier Hayes was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, in terms of your mission, carrying out this Security Council mission, did Brigadier Hayes help or hinder your mission?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Brigadier Hayes was -- I think he interpret the mandate of the Security Council mission like to take the ambassadors for a tour of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not as a mandate to find out what was going on on the ground. And I will explain why. To begin with, Brigadier Hayes refused to take the journalist who came from New York as part of our mission. He sabotaged, boycotted, do not allowing them to enter Srebrenica. Only to get to Zvornik. He almost managed not to let the rest of my delegation arrive in Srebrenica. I went with him first and he said in the next helicopter would follow your colleagues and the press. That didn't happen for two hours while he was negotiating with this Serb colonel Rodic or Radic. What happened, it was suddenly they were caught in this situation that we were going to find out which was the real situation in Srebrenica.
