Because when they were forcing the capitulation on the Bosnians, they never thought that the United Nations Security Council mission was going to visit them and ask questions and ask to be taken to Srebrenica. So, Your Honours, if I tell you that the United Nations forces sequester and got the cameras away from six ambassadors of the United Nations, you will find it difficult to believe. This is what happened. The UNPROFOR, following orders from the Serb side, asked all my colleagues to deliver the cameras because they didn't want anyone with a camera entering Srebrenica. They said that they were filming it. I never seen a film of that. I refused to render mine, and the few photographs there are of that time of Srebrenica are the ones that I took. And I gave the roll to the Reuters people at the time as the only record to show, actually, some of the people, the local people, who were defending Srebrenica, the destruction of the city. And it begs the question: Why would the United Nations prevent photographs taken if they have nothing to hide? If this was not a city under siege? If nothing wrong was happening? Why would the United Nations cooperate with the Serbs in preventing photographs? Not from the journalists they prevented; the journalists never got to Srebrenica. Prevented the ambassadors from taking photographs. That's really amazing and shocking to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to look at your photographs now. We have hard copy and we have colour copies which I think we're going to show the colour copies on the screen because we only have black and white copies. And the ERN sequence is 03514788 to 03514800. So if we can see those now in sequence. Now, firstly, tell me if you recognise these photographs or this --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: This photograph I took at the school where the children had been killed a week before. And when we visited Serbs as sort of a refuge where all women and children and all men were on the floor all over the place in the most crowded building that I ever seen in my life. That's the school in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll clip to the next one now. And there's nothing -- if there's anything to comment on, then please comment; otherwise just let us know if you recognise or not this as being one of your photographs.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I do. That's a Canadian colonel to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. We'll clip to the next one. Now, could you explain who these people are in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. If I make a comment, Your Honour, I don't know whether this officer, which is Colonel Radic, that's his real name or not, but this is talking to us in Zvornik. The one behind is the French ambassador, and I am to his right. He is explaining to me that Srpksa is a new republic in control of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's Republika Srpska. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is that you in this picture?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I am, to -- actually, he's addressing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't been reading the ERNs as we go along. I don't know if that's necessary. Perhaps it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are going to tender them as a group with one exhibit number, then it's okay. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that was my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm taking note of the ERNs myself, I'm taking note down of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it now. But it depends on how you prefer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was planning to tender them all in one exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then we can go to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again is this one of yours?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, this is taken from a United Nations armoured car. You can see the destruction of all the villages and homes, which still -- many of them are still in the same situation because I visited recently during the tenth massacre anniversary of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know if you see in the top right-hand corner near the pylon, do you see the church there?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The Orthodox church. That was not damaged?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It was not. All the minarets were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you referring to Srebrenica or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: In Srebrenica and the surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The next photograph, if you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yeah, these were children, you know, they had signs with the name of my country, France, Russia, Pakistan, and New Zealand and Hungary who were the countries represented by us. You know, desperate people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I think actually in the bottom right-hand corner we see a date. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the bottom right-hand corner, we see in red, 93/4/25. So that would be 25 April 1993.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then the next picture. Was this one of your pictures?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: One of a countless -- they were all destroyed. People were living on the streets. There were no homes, there were no buildings, there were no hospitals. I believe there's only one local doctor who was there. They prevented the doctor from outside to come in. So it was -- you know, a picture of total devastation and sadness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: -- about to take place. Hunger. People were really desperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned a doctor. Did you visit a clinic of any description, a health clinic?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Actually, when we were there, there was no clinic. They were being treated in the soccer field. That's the way they were treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then I think we can take the next pictures fairly quickly. Well, yes, the next one -- yes.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: This is the same Serb colonel. I don't know whether he is indicted here or not. He should have been. He was in charge of the shelling of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I don't know if you can recognise the face on the left or tell us what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The left is a British major, a colonel, at the time who was one of Brigadier Hayes' second in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was he happy with you taking that photograph?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No. He told me that they were filming it. It's difficult to imagine that they're going to film genocide, but that's what they said they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: And the United Nations never ever shown a photograph or a film.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: From your mission?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Not from my mission, not from whatever happened during those years in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then we move to the next 4795. Again, houses which have been destroyed. Do you know who had damaged the houses in Srebrenica that you saw?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: This was the shelling coming from the mountain right in front. As I described before, Srebrenica is like in a valley surrounded by the mountains. And the tanks, the Serb tanks, were on top. And it was -- they shelled them until they destroyed the whole village. It was as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And we move to the next picture. Yes. And again, perhaps for these you can just confirm whether or not you took them, because you've explained already.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. You know, I actually gave a lot of these pictures, all of them, actually, to the Prosecution in the case of Mr. Milosevic because there were -- they would portray the destruction of the whole village of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Here we have 14 photographs. Did you only take 14 photographs?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I took like three rolls of film, and I had an information assistant of mine on my mission who took also photos with my camera. And we gave them to the international journalist when we landed in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But in terms of the photographs you've described giving to the Prosecution, did you give them just he 14 photographs that we see here or did you give them --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No, I -- many more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll keep going through this sequence. Next one 4797, again any brief comments you have.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: That's an armoured car, you know, crossing the certain street. People were piling up in certain areas of the village like the soccer stadium in the lower part of town, the -- we are descending into the village, and of course the closer you were to the mountains, the more destroyed and at risk the people were. So they were all down by the lower part of the city or the village of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think we just have three more.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: This is a cruel example of what was all over. There were no selective targets. Srebrenica in the whole was a target. It was a pure exercise in ethnic cleansing and destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And then the next one. And that's -- do you recognise that building -- can you tell us where in Srebrenica that was roughly.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: That's the lower part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then I think we just have two more. Yes, that one --

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The same, you know. It's another vision from the same terrible situation that the people were living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally 801 we see a house which appears to have no roof whatsoever. Is that a picture you took?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask for an exhibit number for these photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these photos, which number 14 in total, and which go from ERN 03514788 to and inclusive of 03514801 are being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D957.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going back to something else which you told us earlier about, how Brigadier Hayes introduced some Bosnian Serb officers who appeared to be military officers by name, and then he turned to some Bosnians and said "these are also my friends. Did he appear to know who they were or not by name?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I think after Brigadier Hayes introduced each Serb by his rank and name and then he had to his other side the three or four Bosniaks, you know, he realised that he had made a mistake in -- and as an afterthought he said, "And these are also my friends," meaning the victims, supposedly the defenders of the village. As I said before, he was much more familiar with the aggressors than with the victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were those Bosniaks in full uniform as well, full military fig?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: It's really, you know, it's sad to say, they looked really pathetic. One of them had a shotgun and I asked him: What do you do in your life? He said: Well, I used to be a teacher. The other one was a mechanic. They were, to begin with, very poorly dressed. They were not in uniform, and they were very badly armed. I would say they were actually almost disarmed, which was the situation at that part of the world until about 1994, 1995, when things started to change and they got better equipment later on, even though the international community forbid them for a long time to be armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So if I were to -- if you were to be shown a video, part of a video with people in uniform, or bits of uniform, would that change your view about what you saw that day or is that what you saw? Poorly dressed people not in uniform?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The only people that I saw that appeared as defenders were very few, to start with, very few. We called for a meeting, Your Honours, of the village in the middle of the -- of Srebrenica where I addressed the people in the village of why we were there. And I can see it still today when I stood up to speak. At the end of the room there was again the Serb colonel, and on the right there were the three or four Bosniak defenders, one of them the mayor of the city. And I told him, you know, we were there to make sure that they would be protected, that I came under the mandate of the United Nations Security Council that was responsible for the preservation of peace and security in the world, that I would guarantee to them that we will protect them. You know, Your Honours, every time I think about it I flinch, because two years later they massacred 7.000 of them and no one did anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Even though we had said that a massacre would take place. I said it -- it's not today that I'm saying this. I said it in a public meeting of the Security Council that the major massacre would take place, that there was a slow-motion genocide before the eyes of the world. And all those words that we conveyed to the poor people of Srebrenica were a false promise. We made -- the UN and international community carries a major responsibility in encouraging them to stay there, to develop expectations that the world would protect them, and that the UNPROFOR forces would not allow the Serbs to massacre them. And we failed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. In that regard, I have an exhibit which we'll pass up. It's from the Washington Post dated 26th April 1993. And the headline is: "UN delegation visited shell-scared Bosnian enclave Ambassadors back expansion of demilitarised zone around Srebrenica, criticised Serbs." I'm just going to read a part from page 3 of this document where it says reporting on this mission: "It is a snap-shot of hell, said New Zealand's O'Brien who described the winding streets of hillside Srebrenica as packed with people, excrement and trash. During a stop at a school, he said the delegation found 38 children in one small room sitting on mattresses with their mothers. Some had oozing sores, he said." Pausing there, is that what you described and the photograph which you took? Was that of that school?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. You know, I think that the human misery that is witnessed there, it's very difficult to summarise in words. And that was the closest that I could come up at that time to describe the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this here, O'Brien is -- can you just explain for us who New Zealand's O'Brien is?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: O'Brien was a permanent representative of New Zealand and was part of the delegation, Ambassador O'Brien.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And then it goes on: "The Serbs have forbidden doctors from getting to the city, O'Brien said, adding that only one doctor remained in Srebrenica. Arria said the water, electricity, and medical problems amounted to a slow process of killing people. Srebrenica is like an open jail, a slow genocide. You can kill people by bullets, shelling, or sickness. In Srebrenica, the Serbs are killing people by sickness." Do you recall whether you made those comments?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly did. I did them in Srebrenica, in Zvornik, in the official room where the United Nations Security Council meets, and in front of the international press. I felt at the time, as I feel now, that the UNPROFOR forces were more in prison getting over with the situation there regardless of the outcome because Srebrenica was becoming like a thorn on the side of the UNPROFOR forces. And they were more concerned for that than for the misery affecting the people of that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say that "Srebrenica was becoming a thorn in the side of the -- of UNPROFOR," did that affect or not the attitude of UNPROFOR towards the defenders of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Your Honours, you must be familiar with the name Akashi. Akashi was a representative of the Secretary-General in Bosnia. Akashi considered, he said it, that the people in Srebrenica were contrabandists, smugglers, I mean, in a way saying not worth fighting for. I wonder whether Mr. Akashi thought that they would export something from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: General Morillon is quoted by his own aide-de-camp, telling the Serb general that he will help them to get rid of that nest of terrorists in Srebrenica without additional cost to you. With that kind of a perception that those gentlemen had on Srebrenica, it must be very clear they were not willing to do much about it. And diplomatically Srebrenica was closer to Greater Serbia. It was an appealing, appetising part of the territory that the Serbs wanted that was part of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll ask for an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, Mr. Jones. This document with ERN M0011807 to 810 is being given Defence Exhibit Number D958.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And overall, given what you saw on your mission and what you told us about this Colonel Rodic, about the behaviour of Brigadier Hayes, the triage, et cetera, what did that show you about what was actually in charge on the ground in Srebrenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No doubt that the Serbs were in full control. Even more, when we were on the way to Srebrenica, we were stopped by a group of Serb soldiers near what they called Charlie checkpoint, something outside Sarajevo. And they stopped us and put a tank with the cannon facing the vehicle where I was, which was the first vehicle on the mission. And even though we had 30 or 40 journalists behind our armoured cars, one Serb sergeant or corporal held two British generals, three French colonels, and I don't know, countless Swedish and Danish soldiers that were there, we were about 40 armed cars and tanks. And one sergeant, Serb sergeant stopped us for two hours, threatened us, and all the time the behaviour of the people who were protecting us were so subordinate that I'm sure that their own countrymen saw them they would be really very ashamed of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've referred to your press conference in Zvornik and the matters which you dealt with there, and I'm not going to go over that again now. Except for one part, and it may help if we refer to paragraph 344 of your statement, it's at page 46, if you still have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And it's -- in that paragraph 344 you say, and it's about, I don't know, maybe 20 lines down: "The Serbs are effectively running a concentration camp policed by UNPROFOR while they act as wardens of this open jail. Meanwhile the slow-motion genocide to kill them gains speed. Srebrenica is a symbol of resistance, a symbol of defiance by their courageous people." Now, firstly, do you recall that that was something which you said in Zvornik in your press conference?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. I said that when we returned from -- when we came out of Srebrenica and we landed in Zvornik right after coming out of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in your statement in -- testimony in Milosevic, you said how President Izetbegovic was sometimes called intractable by the international community, and you compared him to Benes, the prime minister of Czechoslovakia who was also criticised before the Second World War for not covering up his country and giving part of it to the Nazis. Do you recall that firstly?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Very much so. Very much so. Actually, even Lord Owen, who was quite a gentleman, was very disdainful. They called him Izetbegovic and never addressed him as President Izetbegovic. And I complained to Owen officially that every time they referred to Bosnia they call them the Muslim side and not the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And of course President Izetbegovic did not play the role, as I said at the beginning, in the script -- he didn't follow the script and roll down and play dead. And he was a leader of his people to resist the invasion of another country.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were the defenders of Srebrenica regarded as a nuisance by the international community for the same reason?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely. I don't know, Your Honours, if I can indicate something, which to me set the stage for the massacre. When we -- the non-aligned members of the council, when the things started in Srebrenica, proposed a safe area resolution, I personally was one of the drafters. It is one of the things I feel sorry in my life for having suggested that, because we brought the idea to create protected areas, which the French call it "securite," and in Spanish it's "protegido," and in English protected. Had different meanings, which is one of the problems of the Security Council. Because could be different interpretations according to the interests of each party, and that's a very serious matter. On the second resolution after our mission, which is 836, I personally asked Madam Ogata to give us some guidelines of what the safe area should be, and she did. And she also sent a copy to the secretariat. So we asked the Secretary-General to prepare some -- a paper for us and if my memory doesn't fail me, on May 28th, 1993, the secretariat circulated what we call at the UN a non-paper, which were the guidelines of the safe area. That was circulated to us in the informal consultation room, which is the size of this room, where there is no press, no one except the members of the Security Council, and no records are kept. To my surprise, I got my copy, and a few minutes later someone from the secretariat came up and picked up the copies that were on the table. There were only a few ambassadors; I had come earlier. And you have to say: What happened? Four days later the -- France, the UK, and Russia promoted the resolution for the safe areas without waiting for the first time in the history of the United Nations, to adopt a resolution without the recommendations or objections of the Secretary-General. The UN Security Council acts after they hear the Secretary-General. In this case, they decided to go ahead without a report. And one would ask: Why? Because they knew that the report prepared by the secretariat, some of the secretariat people, and Madam Ogata, had three fundamental points. First, that should be the will to protect them militarily and to protect them to any extreme; second, that the safe area should have access in and out, humanitarian, water, electricity, public services, so it was the opposite of what became. I am sad to tell you, Your Honours, that that day was actually the death sentence of the people in Srebrenica because the world thought that the Security Council was going to defend them; no, it was a charade. They were not willing to defend them. That's why they could not wait to have that report as part of the resolution, because if that report had been part of the resolution, they would have to protect them militarily and do the opposite of what happened in Srebrenica. And I repeat to you, that day the Secretary-General withdrew the paper at the request of some of the permanent members. If I remember well, the Secretary-General was in London and some of the gentlemen called him and said, You have to withdraw the paper, and he withdrew it. That paper is mentioned in the new Secretary-General Kofi Annan's report of the massacre of Srebrenica when he refers to that paper. Had that paper been part of the resolution the international community would have had to take a position, we will defend it or not but not to appear to be doing something for the people who were massacred actually two years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one matter. In fact, I think if you look at page 53 of your statement, paragraphs 387 onwards, is that dealing, at least in part, with what you just told us about this non-paper, the paper that was never officially presented is referred to in paragraph 389. Is that describing what you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And following -- following what you've just described, did you hear permanent members saying that in fact there was no duty to defend the safe area?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely. The interpretation made, even though it was chapter 7 of the Security Council, the United Nations charter, they didn't feel any obligation to defend them and they did not defend them; and we know the consequences of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to turn briefly back to your report which I think now has an exhibit number, which is D956.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's D956. And it's the report or letter of transmittal and then your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know if the witness has that in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mission report, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this introduction refers to Resolution 819. And when we see that resolution, we see that the language in fact condemns: "Hostilities by Bosnian Serb parliamentary units, the interdiction of Bosnian Serb -- by Bosnian Serb paramilitary units of humanitarian assistance convoys." In other words, there's a reference to the Bosnian Serbs in particular. You told us how before the language tended to be morally neutral. Can you explain what happened with this resolution?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: This was the first time in two years of the Bosnian tragedy that the Security Council was forced to admit that there was an aggressor. Why did it happen? In our mission there were representatives of France, for example, who had opposed that throughout the process. But the French delegate in the mission signed the report, so they couldn't contradict their own report. And this -- that was an eventful element for the first time to recognise by the Security Council that there were not two parties, but there was one party was the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm just going to turn back to your statement briefly. Before I do so, I want to clarify one matter in your statement and it's fairly trivial, but I want to clear it up. If you go to paragraph 74, I think it is -- 78 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was precisely among the reasons that I placed my first objection on the record. If there is something within the report that is not either truthful or may be something that after a period of time Ambassador Arria would say that he would have changed his mind or was not explained correctly, I think that that certainly can be asked of him. But to preface any question that we're now going to ask him about a report that so far his evidence has been is truthful and correct so far as he remembers, that there's a part in here that might need a correction, prefacing that is not only just a form of leading the witness but is a bit of a misuse of his statement, which we had feared. If he says something contradictory, then we can go to the statement and show where possibly that is not reflected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you're running --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is absolutely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I think you're running, Ms. Sellers, because I don't know what the question is going to be. Because so far I have followed closely this series of questions that Mr. Jones put with reference to particular parts. I don't think there has been an abuse of the process that we sort of regulated in the first place. So let's wait and see what the question is. If it's going to be a leading question, I will stop Mr. Jones, you can rest assured. But I don't know what question he is going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Pardon me, I might have been misunderstood. I'm not saying at this point that the question is leading, just seeing Mr. Jones having prefaced the question, that he's going to clear up something, it might be trivial. I'm unaware at this point, is there something that Ambassador Arria would re-do on his statement. The point that I'm trying to make, Your Honour, is that we just can directly ask Ambassador Arria: Did you -- a question: Did he say that this is what happened. Now, let's go back to your statement is that contradicted? The appearance that we're clearing this up first we're telling him that we're about to clear this up is rather indicative. I don't want to relabour the point, Your Honour, because Mr. Jones did say it's a trivial matter, but I do want to say that, in essence, it's not the proper way, I believe, to use his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't tend to agree with you at this point. But let's see what the question is. And if it's not regular, I'm sure we'll put Mr. Jones in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, you'll see it's a ridiculous objection, and it's utterly trivial and we've wasted two minutes, and you'll see that in seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Paragraph 78 has a one sentence and in the middle of that sentence we see, in brackets: "How can you support this assertion?" Now, obviously that's not a statement -- that's not a sentence which belongs there. My question is simply this: Is that a question posed by an OTP investigator which simply got left in the statement by mistake? It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Am I being asked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour, it is -- I find it difficult to lead me in question when I have been a participant and an observer and a witness to these issues which I knew so well and know so well. Yes, that was a question put to me by the Prosecution at the time, whether I would be able to sustain it, and I said yes, I did. I did so at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. It was simply to ask him if he could cross out those words because they're obviously someone else's markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, basically we have a confirmation from him that these are not words spoken by him but someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You'll see, it was absolutely trivial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, please, because time is pressing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we've looked at your report, and we were looking at the Resolution 819 which you've told us about how there was no longer moral equivalent phrasing being used, in essence, because you had been on the ground and seen the situation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And at paragraph 17 of that report it stated the following: "There is no doubt that had this agreement not been reached, most probably a massacre would have taken place." And then you go on in paragraph 18 to say how Srebrenica is the equivalent of an open jail. I was just going to ask you about the -- that reference to a massacre, that a massacre would have taken place. Is that -- that's something you stand by in your report?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. It is based on the military information provided to us on the ground by the three officers, Wahlgren, Morillon, and Hayes, that the Serbs were going to really exterminate. It just took longer than we thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, are you familiar with the report prepared by the Secretary-General, and by that I mean Kofi Annan rather than Boutros-Ghali, regarding the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Very much so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we're going to distribute a copy of the front page and then one paragraph from that report. Thank you. So this document reads: "United Nations General Assembly, 15 November 1999," and it's a report of the Secretary-General pursuant to General Assembly Resolution 53/35, the fall of Srebrenica. And we just have an extract from one photograph because it's a very long report, obviously. And in particular, I want to draw your attention to the following; it's the last two sentences. It says: "The Serbs repeatedly exaggerated the extent of the raids out of Srebrenica as a pretext for the prosecution of a central war aim, to create a geographically contiguous and ethnically pure territory along the Drina while freeing up their troops to fight in other parts of the country. The extent to which this pretext was accepted at face value by international actors and observers reflected the prism of moral equivalency through which the conflict in Bosnia was viewed by too many for too long." Now, my question is, you referred to moral equivalency. Do you share any of the sentiments expressed there?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely. I understand that you all must know that this is the first time ever that a Secretary-General of the United Nations has ever made a report of that nature, bringing to the surface the failures of the international community and of the UN, which was in the case of Srebrenica and Rwanda, and I concur with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you said earlier that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I'll ask for an exhibit number, please, for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become D959.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You said earlier how events such as the assassination of the deputy prime minister of -- Turajlic and other events created this culture where basically the Serbs, as you said, could get away with murder. And you referred a couple of times to comments by General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask if the exhibit could be shown -- the exhibit. If the witness could be shown Exhibit P510, Prosecution Exhibit P510. And actually, while that's being located:

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you in fact look into whether a proper investigation was conducted in the matter of Mr. Turajlic?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR forces, UNPROFOR command, prepared a report of the assassination, because that's what it was, of the deputy prime minister. And it was circulated to the members of the Security Council. I immediately sent that report to two former prosecutors, national prosecutors, one in Canada and one in the United States, asking them for their legal opinions about these proceedings. I sent copies to the Prosecution during the Mr. Milosevic trial of the opinion of those two distinguished jurists in which actually UNPROFOR didn't do any kind of a serious review of the situation. I complained constantly on this to the Security Council. Boutros-Ghali offered all the time to present the report, and to present the report, which they never did. And of course the message, like I said to you before, to the Serbs that the climate of impunity that prevailed would allow them from then on to do anything. And I assigned so much importance to that fact because the aggressiveness climbed after that rapidly and ended in what we know in Srebrenica, which people tend to see as one massacre. It was a massacre that took place within two or three years and accumulated in time. I've always been against individualising the one individual massacre. This was a massacre of people during a pro-Serb evacuation. Like when we speak of the Holocaust, you don't speak of the Holocaust of 1944 or 1943, we speak of the Holocaust. Here is a massacre of people in that part of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you just two last matters then. In this exhibit which you have there, and it's pages 3467 and 3468.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. It's in that document which is on the ELMO. During the course of proofing, did I in fact show you an extract from a diary?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that the diary? Yes. And when you were referring earlier to comments made by General Morillon, are you referring to what we see on page 3468 -- I should say for the record 3467 has 15 March, 1520 hours, Potocari, General Milovanovic, General Morillon, and Colonel Dolimir or Polimir. And then the second page that we see the words "I know you wish to clean out this nest of terrorists. I will do it for you and save you many, many casualties." Is that what you're referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. I was really horrified to read that, and even more so to read the explanation that General Morillon expressed such a statement that get rid of that nest of terrorists at no cost to you, because that was a language that the Serbs understand better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that consistent or not with the attitudes of UNPROFOR officers, what we see there?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: There is no doubt that corroborates what the Bosnian government and representative told us countless times. Your Honours, the amount of statements sent by the Bosnian president, and at the time the Bosnian Ambassador Sacirbey at the Security Council, almost every day on what was taking place reached a point that some of the permanent members would come to the Security Council and say, Oh, another letter from Mr. Izetbegovic. Oh, another letter from Sacirbey. And they were saying yesterday 75 people were killed, 200 people were killed, so many of them were raped. Oh, another claim from the Bosnians. I saw this. I didn't read about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And then finally a last exhibit we have, it's the letter of Tadeusz Mazowiecki. Firstly I'll just ask you, do you know Tadeusz Mazowiecki, the special rapporteur of the Commission on Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. I had the privilege to meet him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you aware that he resigned from his post because of the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That he resigned following the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now this is General Assembly Security Council document 18 September 1995, and it's annex 1 that there's a letter from Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If Your Honours will give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, in this document Mazowiecki compares the situation in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the fight in Poland against totalitarianism and states that the very stability of international order and the principle of civilisation is at stake over the question of Bosnia. I want to ask you whether you saw the conflict in those terms of collective security?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You know, the fact that Mr. Mazowiecki would make such a statement should have made a greater impact because of whom he is. And I absolutely concur with him in his views -- not only concur with him, I express similar thoughts while I was a member of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I think I would simply ask for an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will become Defence Exhibit D967.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you recall yourself using words from Henry V to describe the UN's role in all of this?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, the day the Security Council passed that infamous resolution, offering protection that they were not willing to do or to provide, I said at the end of my intervention, it is in the public statement, something to the effect that: I hope when you look backwards you wouldn't have to recall Henry the V in Shakespeare. It is nothing but a shame, eternal shame, on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask the Court give me five minutes' indulgence because we have just one or two issues to check on prior to proceeding with this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Do we need to stay here or should we walk out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you feel more comfortable if we suspend the sitting --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could we suspend it for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can confer in privacy with Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ambassador, if you bear with us a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With pleasure, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Break taken at 2.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you wish to cross-examine the witness, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thanks again for the Trial Chamber's indulgence on this small break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you think you will take?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try and complete Ambassador Arria today, and I think that I will be able to conclude my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ambassador Arria.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I have a couple of preliminary questions, but given the time constraint my questions might really appear to jump around to different things that you've testified about today, so I'd ask that you bear with me so that we will be able to complete your cross-examination. My first question, Ambassador, is that certainly you understand that you have been asked to testify in the case of the Prosecution versus Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did you meet Naser Oric when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I think you are also aware that the Prosecution's case concerns crimes that were committed against Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992. You're aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Of alleged crimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And this brings me to the first area that I wanted to get your clarification on. Now, you've mentioned that Bosnia-Herzegovina became a member of the United Nations of the General Assembly in March 1992. Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, with Bosnia-Herzegovina becoming a full-fledged member with all that entails within the United Nations, can you confirm to the Trial Chamber that that meant that all the inhabitants, all of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would then, via their country, be recognised as members of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Once the General Assembly admits a member, the Security Council reviews the procedure, which we did, and approve the membership, and of course it includes the whole of the population, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And because of the unfortunate ethnisation of the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you would agree that both what is referred to as Bosnian Muslims or Bosniaks and Bosnian Serbs were the inhabitants and the citizens of the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time period, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: When we admitted, we called them "Bosniaks," "Bosnians," never call them any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the other -- the question I want to ask you related to this is that since you've recognised that there was aggression, in particular coming in from what would have been known as Serbia and Montenegro, the former Yugoslavia, into now the sovereign territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you would look at that aggression, in essence, a war of one state against another state that was a member of the United Nations. Am I correct in understanding that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Not precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Please clarify then.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You had an aggressor, which was a state, and you had their intermediaries within -- like, the paramilitaries within the territory. So it was a state aiding and abetting and supporting also forces within another country. So it was a mixture of the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So this mixture would almost be a mixture of war between states and a war among a state, if I'm correctly understanding what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You are the lawyer. I think it would be difficult to make that case precisely. It was definitely a war of aggression on the side of the Serbs. Now, whether it was a state against state war, that remains probably for you to clarify to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say the Serbs now, are we speaking of the nation of Serbia and Montenegro, or are we speaking of Serbs from a different geographical location?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Always when I refer to them, I refer to them from Serbia and Montenegro. Yes, thank you for asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to clarify that. Sir, you've mentioned in your testimony today that this idea of victims on parity with aggressors, and I'd just like a little clarification of that terminology before I move into the body of my cross. When you're talking about victims, are you talking about Bosniaks or are you talking about Bosnian Muslims who are Bosniak? Could you just clarify that or are you talking about civilians, members of the army? I'm just uncertain with your use of the terminology "victims."

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Basically I think the length of my position before during Mr. Milosevic and today, when I speak of the victims, I'm speaking of what has become the regular language here in this Tribunal to refer to them as the Muslim part of the equation. And I -- you probably recall that today I said that was not the way to address the members of that country before the conflict started.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So would you recognise that it would be proper when one speaks of victims that one could speak also of individual victims of a crime that might have occurred during war?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. I would have to say yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And can I take it that you would probably also agree with the proposition or maybe from your point of view the fact, that at times there were Bosnian Serb or Bosniaks who were Bosnian Serbs who might have been individual victims of crimes committed during this war at this time period?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You know, I've been posed that question before in a different context, and this would be like criticising the people of Delft for defending themselves against the Germans at the time. And of course when you attack somebody, you run the risk of being hurt, too. But you have to see it from the perspective of the victims who were being aggressively attacked. But, yes, I understand your question, and of course there must be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir. I'm taking your answer to be a yes?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thanks. And also in this same realm, I'm certain you who were one of the founders, if one could say, of the commission of experts that's seen as very important work that you would agree that during this conflict we had individual perpetrators of crimes who could have come from any of the countries involved and through the ethnisation any of the ethnic groups involved?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, I heard the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Would you precisely tell me what am I going to agree with at this time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, you would agree perpetrators could have been either Bosnians -- Bosniaks were Bosnian Serbs or Bosnian Muslims or persons who came from Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I would have to agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to come a little bit closer to some of the concrete work that you did in Bosnia and particularly in Srebrenica in 1993. And if you would just assist us by giving us the exact dates that you were in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I was just reminded that it was April 24. I have the reports in my hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The dates are shown in the first annex after page 13 on the report, if I remember well, from the 23rd to the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He said in evidence he was there on the 25th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, you know, that I understand, and I just wanted to at this point under -- have Ambassador Arria to remind us the length of the mission and the time period spent in Srebrenica. It's the point of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I understand you better now. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you just confirm that you were in Srebrenica on one day, that day was April 25th, 1993, out of the three- or four-day period of the entire mission.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You know, that question was posed to me exactly by Mr. Milosevic. And of course I'm sure you don't want to imply the same thing that he did. He did imply to me openly that I had been there for too short a time to really provide an expert opinion. I told Mr. Milosevic that it didn't take but a few hours to see human misery and destruction. You had -- you have to live with that. On the contrary, it seems that the people from the United Nations who saw that for a long time got used to the idea of seeing misery without reporting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ambassador Arria.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Not to confuse the witness and the panel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I appreciate you not readily implying that Mr. Milosevic and I have the same intent. My intent was precisely to see your time period was there. My next question, therefore, would go to the mandate that the mission had. Was that mandate written prior to going to Srebrenica or the mission? Or did that mandate evolve through your experience in Srebrenica, the things you saw?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We had a very general description of the mission. This mission was agreed at 2.00 in the morning. We left 24 hours later. And actually, we were given authority to design our trip any way we saw fit for, but of course the purpose of the mission was to report to the Security Council. They didn't tell us to stay a week there. Just tell me, tell us what's going on there. The UNPROFOR forces, they don't want us to spend too much time in Srebrenica, to come to your point, they wanted us to spend more time in Zagreb, the fighting in Zagreb, or spend more time in Kiseljak, which is the headquarters of UNPROFOR. We wanted to be in Srebrenica, and they made everything possible for us not to be there and to be there as little as possible. You will recall that I said to you, I said to Their Honours, that Hayes interpreted our mission like a tour. He thought that putting us in a flak jacket and a helmet would make us very happy to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that part of the testimony. So am I to understand that the mandate of what you were to do in the Srebrenica part of your mission was something that was fairly wide open from the point of view of the members of the delegation? Would that be correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And also is it something that expanded or conformed to do what you saw or what you wanted to know or things that might have popped up during this 24-hour period?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We were not prepared to see what we saw. You see, we were under the false illusion and cover-up that our own colleagues in the Security Council had told us that the city was under siege. They didn't tell us that they had been suffering for four months, that Madam Ogata had warned of a massacre. They didn't tell us that there was no electricity, water, nothing, no medics, and hat they were trapped, as Mr. Karadzic had said once, trapped like rats. So we were not prepared to see anything of that sort, so to us it came as a shock.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Ambassador. And along those lines, in terms of preparation, you've testified that it appears that there was almost some type of block-out on information coming to you and the Security Council about Srebrenica. Now, please correct me, are you referring to Srebrenica the town or Srebrenica the municipality, in terms of the block-out of information?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I'm referring to the whole country. But the hottest spot at the time was the municipality of Srebrenica. But actually, the information on the whole process was not coming, like torture was not being reported, concentration camp was not being reported. So Srebrenica was added, and I dare to say if it had not been for this British journalist, I think he was shot later on in the leg or the arm, I think Birtley is his name, probably would have waited longer. We would not have known what was taking place in Srebrenica. Maybe they would have massacred them earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Sellers, if you please, I'd like to interrupt you here to clear one thing up following your very important questions in regards where are we talking -- what the witness is talking about. You recorded here in the annex the itinerary that on the 25th you arrived in Srebrenica and you had a meeting with Colonel Rodic, Major Popovic, Major Civic and Major Madzic. Where did you meet these four presumably -- not presumably, are all army people. Where did you meet these? In the town of Srebrenica itself or outside the town but inside the Srebrenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The day that we left Kiseljak for Srebrenica, surprisingly I land in an old soccer field, old airport was soccer field. I asked Hayes, Why are we landing? Well, I have to talk to some people here. That was Zvornik. And we landed, and that's where we were welcomed by these Colonel Radic or Rodic. And actually what was happening he was negotiating permission for us, the UN Security Council, to enter the village of Srebrenica, which we thought had not been capitulated. That was still under siege. So this lasted about two hours. I mean, they were delaying this as much as they could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's why. And then they flew in the helicopter with us, and in the same helicopter, it was a French helicopter, into Srebrenica, this gentleman that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you -- yes. You met them in this soccer field in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Zvornik and then in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then in Srebrenica. Yes. And then you show here briefing by Lieutenant Colonel Geburt, Jean-Claude Amiot, Francois Bellon, and Jose Maria Mendiluce. Did you have this briefing with these four gentlemen at the same time, together, or separately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some together, some separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- and the place where you had the briefing, would that be in Srebrenica town or before you reached Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before Kiseljak, Zagreb, Sarajevo, and then Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's perfect. Thank you. Judge Eser. I apologise to you, Ms. Sellers, but I think this was important to clarify for our understanding at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarification, we already had some confusion with regard to the term "municipality." Now, what do you mean with municipality? In your testimony you only spoke of what I would describe as the town, the valley, of Srebrenica. When you talk of municipality, do you also think of other villages or hamlets around the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a good point, Your Honour. Yes, we always -- well, we want to refer to the area of Srebrenica. It is -- because the people that live around it were also affected -- actually, they came to live on the town where there were less or relatively more protected than being on the outer part of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As a matter of fact, that leads into one of the next questions that I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You talked in your testimony about villages and homes in Srebrenica. And I wanted to ask: In terms of villages, other than the physical town of Srebrenica, was it part of your mandate or did you involve this into your mandate to go out to other villages in the municipality, opstina, of Srebrenica or not?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Probably you don't know that our mission went beyond Srebrenica; that was the reason we met Mr. Karadzic in Belgrade. That's the reason we met in the centre with Mr. Boban in Split. So actually was to see what was going on in the battleground in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we also saw Tudjman, President Tudjman, at the time. So it went beyond -- and that -- we decided whom to meet and whom not to meet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. So in terms of deciding who to meet and not to meet, that resided purely with the delegation?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me possibly rephrase my prior question because I understand that you had meetings with various people, apart from what I would call the Srebrenica part of your mission. Back to the Srebrenica part of your mission, did you visit villages in the Srebrenica municipality as part of the Srebrenica part of your mission? This is what I would like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Thank you for asking that. Yes. Thanks to Mr. Mendiluce, who knew the area very well because it was Madam Ogata's, I insisted to be taken around and outside the village proper of Srebrenica, and that's why I can state to you today, as I did yesterday, that we saw the surrounding area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And could you please inform the Trial Chamber what were the names of those villages that you were able to visit out -- within Srebrenica municipality but outside the city or town, the town or village of Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You are straining and forcing my memory, especially for very complicated names, which are -- for a Latin speaker it is difficult to pronounce, even today, to pronounce Srebrenica. Probably I am doing it incorrectly. But I can tell you in the report there are mentions, and at the time I knew them very well. But I assure you I saw them, and precisely we went to see where the Serb tanks were deployed. So in order for us to see them, we have to go all around and behind the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. So, sir, those names are contained within your report, the names of the villages that you visited outside of the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes, and there are -- they must by the position. They are also included in the Secretary-General's report of the massacre of Srebrenica. And at the time we didn't consider it necessary, because we spoke of Srebrenica as an area rather than a specific village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. So therefore, your visit to the villages surrounding the town, the reason for that was to look at the different Serb military positions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Both. One, two see where they were placed because, according to the resolution, they should not have been there; they should have been withdrawn. And I must tell you, there was no villagers, there was no one there; there was only destruction. That I said in the Security Council is where we understood that "ethnic cleansing" meant. You know, ethnic cleansing was a word in a document in the Security Council, but when you see houses that were put bombs to destroy the roofs so nobody could live there is when you get the grasp. When you see they killed even the animals, sheep, et cetera, killed there is when you realise ethnic cleansing. So I was more interested to witness that than to recall the names of specifically of destroyed towns around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could possibly jog your memory, and certainly tell me if you don't remember. I'd like to ask you the names of a couple of villages to see if you went to see them. Did you go to Ratkovici, sir?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: See, you would have to jog my memory. I would not be able to tell you exactly because I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you -- maybe one village might come back. Did you go to Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Well, I went to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You went to Potocari, yes. Okay?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Is it -- you see, I hardly remember how to pronounce it, but that's one of the places.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Do you remember going or did you have as your mandate to go to Jezestika?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Jezestica.

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Thank you. It's difficult sometimes to remember. As I told you, our mandate was expanded. It was -- I was the head of the mission, so I mean it was agreed with my colleagues what should we do and not do. And we were not collecting, as I told you, names of populations; we were collecting data and information was -- of the tragedy that was evolving there, and I hope you will excuse me for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If that was the mission, then certainly this is what the Trial Chamber wants to hear. Maybe I can assist in your memory. These -- the location of Jezestica, [indiscernible], is in the Bratunac municipality. And I would like to know: As part of your Srebrenica visit did you go to the Bratunac municipality and visit -- I'm going to name the other towns. You've mentioned Jezestica. Also I'll mention now Fakovici, Radijevici, Bjelovac, Divovici, Sikirici, Kravica, or Siljkovici. Did you remember going to any of those towns or villages as part of your Srebrenica visit, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's going to tell you that everywhere he went to ended in "ici," Ms. Sellers, and therefore he cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the sake of the record, I guess he would have to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer. I mean, I think it will only make it more confusing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I concur with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Then, Ambassador Arria, did you have, as part of the mandate or evolving mandate with your mission, to speak to inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in particular civilians who might be, what is called Bosnian Serbs, in relationship to things that have occurred in the Srebrenica municipality in 1992? Was that part of your mandate?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: We made it our mandate and -- so much so, Your Honours, that we met with Mr. Karadzic in Belgrade, which should tell you something that he was dispatching from Belgrade. And actually, we met with him on the first day of the sanction that we had on former Yugoslavia, and we met with the most prominent or infamous one of that part. And he told us that Srebrenica would have water, electricity, services, doctors within 24 hours. It took them three years. And he had to be forced by outside forces to do it. So, yes, we spoke to -- like, we spoke, as I said before, to Mr. Boban, on the Croat side; Mr. Tudjman. You see, this mission was not sent by the Bosniaks; this mission was sent by the United Nations Security Council. So this mission was made up of six Ambassadors from very different countries. So we're not on the mandate of what you would call today the Muslim side. We were sent by the Security Council. So it was an even-handed objective mission. That the fight is stronger on one side than the other is a different matter, and this is a historic record. I think I should be very clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, sir, you are. My question and it might be also, Mr. Karadzic being a civilian, I want to know: Did you speak to any other Bosnian Serb civilians within the Srebrenica municipality? And let me clarify that, civilians who might, themselves, have been refugees, displaced, victims of crimes. Did you speak to any civilian Bosnian Serb Srebrenican villagers during your mandated part of the Srebrenica mess?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Let me respond the following way, which is a factual way. We saw people suffering in the street, because I told you fundamentally women and old men. I did not stop to ask: Are you a Serb? Are you a Bosniak? Are you a Croat? We saw the people suffering. I mean, we didn't ask them for -- identify themselves to us. The only Serbs officially that I can recall are these Radicik -- I'm sorry, the Radic or Rodic gentleman who were there. Because on the other side -- actually, even what you would call the Muslim side, they didn't look like soldiers; we didn't know what they were. One, as I told you, a mechanic, a teacher, those were the only ones that we actually spoke to. So we were even in that. Now, when the people were suffering in the streets, we didn't ask them to identify themselves to us, but I heard mothers, brothers, boys talking they haven't eaten in so many days and have water and have electricity, et cetera, et cetera, we wouldn't ask to identify where the misery was coming from. I don't know if I make myself clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, if I can just paraphrase then I would say that it wasn't a mandate of the mission to speak to Bosnian Serb civilians who might have been refugees or -- that you just spoke to people who were present in the town of Srebrenica, those civilians?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: As I said to you the mandate was to be an objective appraisal of the situation. No one told us or I didn't tell my colleagues or my colleagues didn't tell me, now we must interview a Serb or a Bosniak or a Croat, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I do understand. One of the last questions in terms of a bit of geography, and this will not deal with names but basically miles or kilometres. Do you know how many kilometres or miles outside of the town of Srebrenica that you visited, if you could kind of say the distance or the time it took to get to the places?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: You know, on the hilly side, that's the way you were going around. We were for an hour going around in armoured car; armoured cars do not go very fast, but they go faster than tanks. You do not jog my imagination, but I would have to speculate my imagination, how many miles. But I would say, you know, going around the mountains, how many, I would say around 15 kilometres outside of -- outside of the area because where we saw Mendiluce, said to me at one side, the tanks over there, ask them to take you there. And it took us about half -- you know, about 20 minutes, half an hour to get on top of that mountain. Not because of the distance but how difficult it was to get to the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You've testified that there was not that much information, if I understand correctly, about Srebrenica municipality prior to your arriving on the mission. And is it possible that due to that lack of information about what had happened in the municipality that you were unaware of whether humanitarian aid had arrived in Srebrenica at any time period during 1992 or 1993 prior to your coming?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I just wondering if Ms. Sellers can direct us to where the witness said that there was not that information about Srebrenica municipality prior to you arriving on the mission. Whether she's talking about the municipalities distinct from Srebrenica, I'm not sure but I'd like to know where the witness said that. If I could have a page and line reference, then I'll have a look. I don't recall him testifying to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I unfortunately can't scroll back, but I believe that Ambassador Arria said that not only did they not receive information about Srebrenica. It was the whole country. My impression is that he testified that there didn't seem to be information coming in about the country and then I asked about the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He certainly didn't say, Oh, I had no information about Srebrenica before I got there. The whole tenure of cross -- of examination-in-chief, he explained what his sources of information were on the situation. He didn't say, I went to Srebrenica knowing nothing of the situation there. To the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. At the end of the day, is it going to change history, Ms. Sellers, because we have had reference, evidence already as to what aid was forthcoming and when.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I rephrase the question, just a very direct question, we can get a yes or no and move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ambassador Arria, were you aware that there was humanitarian aid convoy that came to Srebrenica in November of 1992 prior to your mission going to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: When I got to Srebrenica, Mr. Mendiluce, who was the most honest man in the place, said to us no humanitarian assistance had come in. I want to tell Your Honours something -- United Nations Security Council. Yugoslavia, former Yugoslavia, was under sanctions. So when they are under sanctions, there are 50 members. As you know, the 50 members of the Security Council have a commission. If one of them vetoes, each one has a veto power. So every time that Mr. Karadzic wanted to fly away to one meeting or all or whatever, they have to get the permission of the commission. And we always oppose it, to force him to go by ground to take the same risk. And then we -- I learned a procedure by which you try to force them not to approve, for example, the buying of oranges, fruits, from Brazil, whatever, if they didn't let the humanitarian convoys pass by. And Mendiluce was there, confirmed to me that they were not allowed to come in. And actually, hen we were there, and it took almost two years for that to happen. So it was not allowed to go through.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would also like to ask you whether you were aware or not that representatives from Medecins Sans Frontieres came into Srebrenica in December 1992 and then came back in March of 1993. Were you aware that there had been an initial visit by Medecins Sans Frontieres prior to your mission to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: Yes. When I got to Srebrenica as -- you probably recall this morning, I saw a lot of people in white robes, and I thought they were Red Cross or maybe Medecins Sans Frontieres. In the [foreign language spoken] they have been expelled from the village. And now you're telling me that, yes, I recall that I was told that before Medecins Sans Frontieres, before December, had been in the area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, sir, were you aware that there was a war hospital in Srebrenica prior to your coming to the town?

utterances.speaker: DIEGO ENRIQUE ARRIA
utterances.text: I -- yes, I understand there were some -- what you creatively would call a war hospital because there were no hospitals as such. Let's call it a place.
